messages.subject: Posterior of certain parameters appear to be entirely driven by prior
parts:

Could someone help me understand why this is, and how to adjust? 


Let me know if anything needs clarification! 


Thank you,

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: Posterior of certain parameters appear to be entirely driven by prior
parts:
An advisor of Ghislain's here. Thought I'd sex-up his query by describing the context of his data/model:

We're looking at the performance of baseball umpires judging close plays at first base and examining whether different types of attention instructions affect this performance. We show each umpire videos of lots of plays, each play with a slightly different timing between the ball and runner's arrival at the base. For some blocks of plays we instruct the umpires to keep their attention on the base, and for other blocks we instruct the umpires to keep their attention on the baseman's glove. 

For a given umpire and instruction condition we expect the probability of calling a play as "safe" (vs "out") as a binomial draw where the probability is a s-shaped function of the timing between the ball and runner reaching the base. So, high probability of saying "safe" on trials where the runner arrives well before the ball (large positive values of x) and low probability of saying "safe" on trials where the ball arrives well before the runner, and a smooth s-shaped transition between these two extremes.

We use the cumulative normal to achieve the s-shape because the mean-and-sd parameterization allows us to speak directly to bias (shift in the S, indexed by the cumulative normal's mean) and discrimination sensitivity (sharpness of the S, inversely indexed by the cumulative normal's sd). Since we have many umpires, we model this bias & sensitivity hierarchically, and implement an "intercept+-effect" coding to look at the effect of the attention instructions on both bias & sensitivity (again, both hierarchically). All the hierarchical sampling is done via a multivariate distribution, thus including inference on the potential for correlations amongst the parameters across the population of umpires. 

When we run the model against real data, the posterior on the parameters associated with bias seem to be identical to the priors specified for those parameters regardless of said specification. So clearly we've erred somewhere, but we can't quite see where. Any ideas?

Mike

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Posterior of certain parameters appear to be entirely driven by prior
parts:
The model's too complex for me to understand just by looking
at it, but I suspect this may be your problem:

trial_pss[this_obs] <- pss_intercept_per_id[id[this_obs]]
+ pss_effect_per_id[id[this_obs]] * condition[L] ;

Shouldn't that L be this_obs? Otherwise, you get the same observation
for each condition and condition[1:(L - 1)] is otherwise unused.

I also didn't understand why you're doing this:

real<lower=0,upper=pi()/2> zpopulation_pss_intercept_sd;

population_pss_intercept_sd <- tan(zpopulation_pss_intercept_sd);

We generally recommend

real<lower=0> zpopulation_pss_intercept_sd;

and then some kind of weakly informative prior such as

zpopulation_pss_intercept_sd ~ normal(0, 2);

based on the expected scale of the variable for which this is
the scale parameter.

Our general advice is to start with simple models (e.g., no random
effects, fewer predictors, no covariance structure, etc.), fit them to
simulated data to make sure they work, then gradually build them up.
It's much easier to debug that way than starting with a complex
model. As we say in computer science, design top down, code bottom up.
We need to make all this advice clear in the book we're writing! The
manual just presents finished models without showing how we got there.

Also, this coding

vector[4] beta[N];

for (this_id in 1:N)
beta[this_id] ~ multi_student_t(1,zeros,cor) ;

forces N solutions of the cor matrix. It'll be much much
more efficient as

matrix[N, 4] beta;

to_vector(beta) ~ multi_student_t(1, zeros, cor);

Also, one degree of freedom in the T is giving you a very broad likelihood.
So when I meant start simple, remove the correlation structure, use normals,
etc. Then when you add things, you'll know where they go wrong.

- Bob

P.S. I would also strongly recommend against using tabs in computer
programs --- they render differently depending on the context because
there's no universal tab width.

P.P.S. Though it doesn't matter for efficiency, it's easier to replace


for (i in 1:4) zeros[i] <- 0;

with

zeros <- rep_vector(0, 4);

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Posterior of certain parameters appear to be entirely driven by prior
parts: On Mon, May 9, 2016 at 1:40 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

trial_pss[this_obs] <- pss_intercept_per_id[id[this_obs]]
                         + pss_effect_per_id[id[this_obs]] * condition[L] ;

Shouldn't that L be this_obs?  Otherwise, you get the same observation
for each condition and condition[1:(L - 1)] is otherwise unused.

Bingo! That was it, thanks! 


Thanks also for your other comments, a couple responses below:

I also didn't understand why you're doing this:

  real<lower=0,upper=pi()/2> zpopulation_pss_intercept_sd;

  population_pss_intercept_sd <- tan(zpopulation_pss_intercept_sd);

This was to implement the efficient version of a half-cauchy prior on the scale parameter population_pss_intercept_sd. I know that more recently it has been recommended on the list that for scale parameters people abandon the half-cauchy and instead use a normal or >=4 df student-t, but thought I'd switch to the lighter-tail options only if I encountered efficiency issues. Admittedly, the efficient-heavy-tail also makes the code less readable, so we'll probably change it immediately.

matrix[N, 4] beta;

  to_vector(beta) ~ multi_student_t(1, zeros, cor);
Hm, we're getting exceptions during sampling with that version, along the lines of "the dimension of the size of random variable and size of location parameter must match in size"

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Posterior of certain parameters appear to be entirely driven by prior
parts:
It’s not so much a question of efficiency but rather exploration.
If the posterior had tails as heavy as the the tails of the Cauchy 
distribution then HMC would struggle to explore the entirely of
that tail (although it would do far better than other samplers).
In this case the reparameterization would be useful as the
transformed space would feature much nicer tails.

But that would only be a factor here if your model were
non-informative, and even then HMC does okay when a
only a few parameters have heavy tails.  

Ultimately this is an example of premature optimization.
As Bob notes, start simple and build up, adding these
reparameterization tricks only when necessitated by
poor performance.*

*Caveat: in hierarchical models it’s okay to default to
non-centered parameterizations given that most models
add hierarchical structure exactly because the data are
not super informative, which is where the non-centered
parameterization performs best.
